review:
Grow Up is a delightfully cozy and charming little game about a cute red robot trying to rebuild its crashed ship, M.O.M., and get back on track. My experience with it was incredibly pleasant and relaxing. The character controls feel very "floaty," but you can easily write this off as a feature of the alien planet's low gravity. The mechanics are simple and straightforward, allowing you to master the entire game in less than 4 hours. Visually, the low-poly art style works perfectly here. 

However, the late-game progression is where the experience stumbles. Even though unlocking new tools makes collecting crystals easier, hunting down the last remaining crystals can easily eat up more than half of your playtime. The worst part is the payoff: once you return to the ship, the onboard computer simply recounts your achievements, and that’s it. There are no ending animations or satisfying narrative closures. Knowing that such a weak and unrewarding finale awaited me, I chose not to finish it completely, as the tedious grind for the final percentage just isn't worth it.

Still, if you are looking for a chill, low-stress exploration game to enjoy for a few hours without caring about 100% completion, it's definitely worth a look.

[h1]Well, it certainly is more a game now.[/h1]

Grow Up is the sequel to a fine enough tech demo, Grow Home. It expands on the game in nearly every possible way, while presenting some new ideas. It also falls into some of the typical Ubisoft shortcomings.

+ While BUD is still a slippery stumblebot, it feels much refined to control him.
+ The world is genuinely fun to navigate due to an expanded toolkit and several biomes to conquer. 
+ The new major mechanic of scanning plants and placing them (Floroforms) is a neat concept...
+ The different objective means there's multiple means to accomplishing it, be it from above or below. 
+ The music and atmosphere are vastly improved over the original title.

- BUD is somehow more fragile than before, now able to get his block knocked off from new forms of impact that didn't before.
- The challenges are largely crackhorse agility courses. My name isn't Oguri Cup, so I'm frankly not interested. The few actual platforming or navigation courses are neat, though. 
- ...Floroforms become completely moot with enough crystals. 
- Nobody bothered to waterproof BUD in the intervening time. 
- Hades help you should you miss one of the starplant rocks and have to climb down for them.
- One of your abilities is still non-directional, annoyingly enough.

[h1] What is this game? [/h1]
Grow Up is the sequel to the game "Grow Home" - putting the player in the role of the character B.U.D yet again; as he tries to put M.O.M back together after a fatal crash. Along the way you collect seeds for various alien plants and grow "Starflowers" - massive plants that reach in to space.

[h2] Price/replay value [/h2]
Horrible - Bad - [u] Decent [/u] - Good - Amazing

[h2] Achievement hunting [/h2]
Mostly collectible based, some rely on small challenges like bouncing on a Youch 7 times.
"Along for the ride" is probably missable as this requires an uncompleted challenge to fulfill.

[h2] Pros/cons [/h2]
[b] Pros [/b]
[list]
[*]Way more variety in movement
[*]You can choose your order of progression
[*]Eagle eye camera is a nice addition
[/list]

[b] Cons [/b]
[list]
[*]Still incredibly jank 
[*]Crystals don't show properly in eagle eye view
[/list]

[h2] Overall opinion [/h2]
I know this game has very mixed opinions but I personally prefer this one to the first game. The movement (whilst still janky) is a lot better, and the ability to plant seeds at your own volition as well as the glider and air brakes not being consumable, made this game considerably more fun to me. The crystals are slightly easier to find due to the eagle eye camera; but can still be a nuisance when in caves or the like. The increased radar distance does help considerably in spotting them. Starflowers also being optional does make for interesting metroidvania-esque gameplay imo and generally adds flavour to an otherwise fairly bland concept.

[h2] tldr; [/h2]
Better movement, better collectibles, also way easier.

[h2] Should you buy it? [/h2] 
Probably not at full price, but it's a pretty solid game on sale.

I bought this game a long time ago because i saw it on a video of unique short games but never got around to playing it.

It's definitely a very unique game, essentially it's a somewhat physics based game which actual planet physics on a small planet, where you control each hand individually(mainly used for traversal and pulling switches, not much point otherwise lol), and you collect different types of plants which can be used to boost or float you higher, The main goal of the game is to collect all the ship parts so you can go home, but there's a few other collectables around the planet, some unlock new appearances and others make it easier to traverse.

As it's a short game i won't go into too much detail, however, i do want to highlight one really cool feature. Across the planet there are 4 different "star plants", very large vines which you can grab onto and fly onto energy sources to make them grow bigger. Which is really cool, it feels fun flying these tendrils out to other islands!

I like how as you collect more crystals and gear, the world feels much easier to explore, you go from having to find a islands to hop on to climb higher or using star plants to bring yourself higher to being able to rocket around with your hangglider infinitely lol

One somewhat major complaint i had was that the controls can be very janky. For example, you might rocket on your hangglider and it'll inexplicably shoot straight down instead of forward, and sometimes the jetpack whips around weirdly. Another minor complaint is i kinda wish there was more to do,, i feel like a game like this could've been stretched over multiple planets but it can be beaten under 2 hours if you rush it. However i somehow managed to get 11 hours in and i didn't even do any of the challenges lol

Would still recommend it, it's a very cute game!

Much like Grow Home its sequel is a great way to decompress after playing in try hard sweat lobbies all day in whatever the current multiplayer game is.

Grow Up, developed by Reflections, a Ubisoft Studio, serves as the spiritual successor to the quirky and beloved Grow Home. Where the first game introduced players to the charming little robot B.U.D. and his mission to cultivate a massive starplant, Grow Up takes that foundation and expands it into a larger, more ambitious adventure. This time, B.U.D. is tasked with exploring a strange and vibrant alien planet to collect the scattered parts of his spaceship, M.O.M., and the game leans heavily into exploration, physics-driven climbing, and playful experimentation with tools and flora. The result is an experience that feels both whimsical and frustrating, offering moments of joy punctuated by occasional struggles with imprecision.

The core of the game is built around freedom of movement. B.U.D. retains his clumsy, physics-based climbing from Grow Home, but Grow Up introduces several new traversal options that give players more ways to navigate the sprawling environment. The addition of abilities such as a jetpack, a glider, the ability to roll into a ball, and the capacity to scan and replant floraforms significantly broadens how the world can be approached. Each plant has its own unique properties, from launching the robot high into the air to cushioning falls or creating bridges, and scanning them allows players to place these tools wherever they are needed. Combined with the new powers, these mechanics create a sandbox-like sense of discovery, where climbing to the top of an impossibly tall structure or soaring across wide gaps becomes part of the joy.

The world itself is one of Grow Up’s strongest assets. The art style is low-poly and colorful, filled with alien landscapes, floating islands, and vast vistas that encourage curiosity. While the design is simple, it has a unique charm that makes even aimless exploration enjoyable. Climbing to a high altitude and looking out over the terrain provides a sense of accomplishment and wonder, and moments when B.U.D. takes to the skies with a glider or launches off a floraform can be exhilarating. The presentation strikes a balance between playful and serene, with a soundtrack that subtly complements the sense of lighthearted adventure.

Despite its strengths, Grow Up inherits some of the problems of its predecessor and introduces new ones. The physics-based climbing that defines the series is endearing but often unreliable, with B.U.D.’s movements prone to slips, awkward grabs, or unintentional falls. This imprecision can become frustrating during long climbs, as a single mistake often results in plummeting back to the ground and having to repeat progress. The camera, too, can be difficult to manage, particularly in cramped or vertical environments, where keeping track of B.U.D.’s position feels more like a struggle than a natural part of the challenge. These issues don’t ruin the experience but create a layer of friction that some players may find discouraging.

The game’s expanded size is both a strength and a weakness. While there is more to see and do compared to Grow Home, the objectives often boil down to collecting ship parts and completing small challenges, which can sometimes feel like busywork. The novelty of exploration can wear thin when long stretches involve little more than moving from one distant location to another, and the pacing occasionally suffers as a result. The game is relatively short, with a main playthrough lasting around four to six hours, but for players willing to engage with side objectives and collectibles, there is more to discover. Still, the sense of repetition may dampen enthusiasm for some.

Grow Up ultimately succeeds as a lighthearted exploration game with a distinct personality. Its mix of clumsy physics, imaginative floraforms, and colorful environments creates an experience that rewards curiosity and experimentation. It may not offer the precision or depth of more refined platformers, but its charm lies in embracing the unpredictable and finding fun in the chaos of movement. For those who enjoyed Grow Home or simply want a playful, low-pressure adventure, Grow Up delivers enough charm and creativity to make its shortcomings easier to forgive. It is not flawless, but it is memorable for its character, atmosphere, and the freedom it gives players to discover their own path through its alien landscapes.
